13.01.title: Conduction and Fourier's law
13.01.html:
On an April afternoon in Bali the sun heats the west wall of a house to 34 °C on the outside, while the air conditioning holds the room at 26 °C. Heat creeps through the concrete from hot to cold. How much? Heat transfer has three modes: conduction through solids, convection by moving fluids, and radiation. Conduction is the simplest, and one law describes it.

Fourier’s law

In 1822 Joseph Fourier stated that the heat flux (W/m²) is proportional to the temperature gradient and flows down it:

q=−k∇T.

The thermal conductivity k, in W/(m K), is a material property: about 400 for copper, 50 for steel, 1.4 for concrete, 0.13 for wood, 0.035 for mineral wool and 0.026 for still air. Through a plane wall of thickness L with surface temperatures T1​ and T2​:

q=kLT1​−T2​​.

The steady heat equation

Energy balance on a thin slice of the wall says that, in steady state with no heat generated inside, what flows in equals what flows out:

dxd​(kdxdT​)=0.

So kdT/dx is constant through the wall: the flux is the same at every depth. If k is uniform, dT/dx is constant and the temperature profile is a straight line. Where k changes, the slope changes in inverse proportion, but the flux stays the same.

A finite-difference solver makes this concrete. Divide the wall into nodes, write the flux across each face as −kface​(Ti+1​−Ti​)/Δx, and require equal fluxes into and out of every node. That gives a tridiagonal linear system.

Worked exampleThe Bali wall

A 20 cm concrete wall, k = 1.4 W/(m K), outside surface 34 °C, inside 26 °C.

  1. Fourier: q=1.4⋅8/0.2=56.0000 W/m².
  2. The finite-difference solve with 201 nodes gives the same flux at every face (spread 6.5×10−11) and departs from a straight line by less than 10−12 K. Mid-wall it’s 30.0000 °C.
  3. Through 12 m² of wall, 672.0 W enter the room, which the air conditioner must remove.
  4. If the outer half is damp (k = 2.0) and the inner half dry (k = 1.0), the flux is 8/(0.1/2+0.1/1)=53.3333 W/m², still uniform. The joint sits at 31.3333 °C: the profile bends at the joint, with a steeper slope in the less conductive half.

Exercise 1A brick wall in Zürich

A 25 cm brick wall (k = 0.7 W/(m K)) has an inside surface at 18 °C and an outside surface at 2 °C. Find the heat flux and the temperature 10 cm from the inside. How much heat crosses 30 m²?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. q=0.7⋅16/0.25=44.8 W/m².
  2. The profile is linear: T=18−16⋅(0.10/0.25)=11.6 °C.
  3. Through 30 m²: 44.8⋅30=1344 W, a small radiator running nonstop.

13.02.title: Thermal resistance networks
13.02.html:
A mountain hut at 2800 m in the Valais has to stay warm at −10 °C with a small wood stove. Its walls are layered: spruce panelling inside, thick mineral wool, larch cladding outside, and a window. To size the stove you need the heat loss through all of that, and the trick is to treat heat flow like electric current.

Thermal resistance

Fourier’s law for a slab, Q=kAΔT/L, has the form of Ohm’s law I=ΔV/R, with heat flow as current and temperature difference as voltage:

Q=RΔT​,Rcond​=kAL​,Rconv​=hA1​.

The convective resistance describes the thin air layer at each surface, with a surface coefficient h (about 7.7 W/(m² K) inside, 25 outside in wind).

Series and parallel

Layers that the same heat passes through one after another add in series; paths side by side, such as a wall and a window, combine in parallel:

Rseries​=∑Ri​,Rparallel​1​=∑Ri​1​.

Builders quote the U-value, U=1/(Rtotal​A) in W/(m² K): the heat loss per square metre per kelvin. Once the flux is known, the temperature at each interface follows by subtracting qR layer by layer, just like voltage drops along a circuit. The temperatures tell you where moisture might condense inside the wall.

The parallel-path model assumes heat flows straight through each path. Where paths differ a lot side by side, as at a timber stud in insulation, heat also flows sideways, and the simple network becomes an estimate.

Worked exampleThe hut wall

Inside 20 °C, outside −10 °C. Layers: 20 mm spruce (k = 0.13), 120 mm mineral wool (0.035), 24 mm larch (0.13). Surface coefficients 7.7 inside, 25 outside.

  1. Resistances per m²: spruce 0.1538, wool 3.4286, larch 0.1846, plus films 0.1299 and 0.0400. Total 3.9369 m² K/W, so U = 0.2540 W/(m² K) and the flux is 7.620 W/m².
  2. Temperatures from inside out: 20.000, 19.010 (inner surface), 17.838, −8.288, −9.695 (outer surface), −10.000 °C. The wool takes 26 of the 30 K.
  3. A finite-difference solve through the three solid layers between the two surface temperatures gives 7.6202 W/m², the network’s value: Q=ΔT/Rtotal​.
  4. A 12 m² wall with a 2 m² window (U = 1.1): total resistance 0.21097 K/W and heat loss 142.20 W, of which 46.4% goes through the window, though it covers only a sixth of the area.

Exercise 1Doubling the wool

Double the mineral wool to 240 mm. Find the new U-value and the heat loss of the 12 m² wall with its 2 m² window. Was it worth it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. R=3.9369+3.4286=7.3655 m² K/W, so U=0.1358 W/(m² K).
  2. Heat loss: 30⋅(0.1358⋅10+1.1⋅2)=30⋅(1.358+2.2)=106.7 W.
  3. Down from 142.2 W, a 25% cut. The window now dominates (62% of the loss), so a better window would be the next step.

quiz.q: Resistance (m² K/W) of 120 mm mineral wool, k = 0.035. 4 decimals.
U-value (W/(m² K)) for a total resistance of 7.3655 m² K/W. 4 decimals.
Heat loss (W): 10 m² of wall at U = 0.254 and 2 m² of window at U = 1.1, with a 30 K difference. 1 decimal.
A wall and a window side by side combine thermally:
quiz.explain: Two paths for the same temperature difference.
options: As the larger of the two

quiz.q: The largest temperature drop in a layered wall occurs across:
options: The layer with the largest resistance

13.03.title: Cylindrical and spherical conduction
13.03.html:
Wrapping a hot pipe in insulation always saves heat, right? Usually. But wrap a thin electrical wire in plastic and it actually runs cooler than the bare wire. The reason is geometry: in a cylinder, heat spreads through ever larger areas, and adding insulation also adds outside surface for convection to work on.

Conduction through a cylindrical shell

In a long pipe, heat flows radially. The same heat Q crosses every cylinder of radius r, whose area is 2πrL, so Fourier’s law reads Q=−k2πrLdT/dr. Integrating from r1​ to r2​:

Q=Rcyl​T1​−T2​​,Rcyl​=2πkLln(r2​/r1​)​.

The temperature falls logarithmically with radius, not linearly. For a sphere the areas grow as 4πr2, and Rsph​=(1/r1​−1/r2​)/(4πk).

The critical radius

Put insulation of conductivity k on a pipe of radius r1​ and let air with coefficient h carry heat away from the outer surface r2​. Per metre of pipe, the two resistances are in series:

R′(r2​)=2πkln(r2​/r1​)​+2πr2​h1​.

The first term grows with r2​, the second shrinks. Setting dR′/dr2​=0:

rc​=hk​(cylinder),rc​=h2k​(sphere).

At r2​=rc​ the resistance is a minimum, so the heat loss is a maximum. If the bare radius is already larger than rc​, any insulation helps. Hot-water pipes are always in this regime: with foam at k=0.04 and still air at h=10, rc​=4 mm. Thin wires are not: with PVC at k=0.19, rc​=19 mm, so the insulation on a 2 mm wire helps keep it cool.

Worked exampleA coated wire and a hot-water pipe

A 2 mm-radius wire, 40 K above still air (h = 10 W/(m² K)), coated in PVC (k = 0.19).

  1. Bare, it loses 5.0265 W/m. Scanning r2​ in 0.01 mm steps, the loss peaks at 14.6871 W/m at r2​=19.00 mm, and a golden-section search puts the maximum at 19.000000 mm =k/h.
  2. A sphere of radius 1 mm with the same coating peaks at 38.00 mm =2k/h.
  3. A 15 mm copper hot-water pipe (r1​=7.5 mm, 50 K above the air) with foam (k = 0.04): 23.562 W/m bare, 15.125 with 5 mm of foam, 10.466 with 13 mm, 7.906 with 25 mm. Here rc​=4 mm is smaller than the pipe, so every millimetre helps.

Exercise 1A steam pipe

A steel steam pipe has outer radius 30 mm and runs at 160 °C in a 20 °C plant room (h = 12 W/(m² K)). Insulation (k = 0.045) brings it to 80 mm. Find the critical radius, and the heat loss per metre bare and insulated (ignore the steel’s resistance and radiation).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. rc​=0.045/12=3.75 mm, far below 30 mm: insulation helps.
  2. Bare: Q′=2π⋅0.03⋅12⋅140=316.7 W/m.
  3. Insulated: R′=ln(80/30)/(2π⋅0.045)+1/(2π⋅0.08⋅12)=3.4690+0.1658=3.6348 m K/W, so Q′=140/3.6348=38.52 W/m, an 88% cut.

quiz.q: Critical insulation radius (mm) for k = 0.19 W/(m K) and h = 10 W/(m² K).

Critical radius (mm) of insulation on a sphere, k = 0.05, h = 10.

13.04.title: Fins
13.04.html:
A CPU dissipates 100 W from a chip the size of a fingernail. Convection from such a small area can’t carry that away. The solution is to extend the surface with fins: the aluminium spikes on a cooler, the ribs on a motorbike cylinder, the plates of a radiator. A fin works only as well as heat can conduct along it, so its temperature falls with distance from the base, and beyond a certain length extra metal does almost nothing.

The fin equation

Take a fin of cross-section A, perimeter P and conductivity k, in air at T∞​ with coefficient h. On a slice dx, heat conducted in minus heat conducted out equals heat convected from the side, hPdx(T−T∞​). With the excess temperature θ=T−T∞​:

dx2d2θ​=m2θ,m2=kAhP​.

With θ(0)=θb​ at the base and a convecting tip, −kθ′(L)=hθ(L):

θb​θ​=coshmL+mkh​sinhmLcoshm(L−x)+mkh​sinhm(L−x)​.

Heat rate, efficiency, effectiveness

The heat leaving the fin equals what enters its base, q=−kAθ′(0):

q=McoshmL+mkh​sinhmLsinhmL+mkh​coshmL​,M=hPkA​θb​.

For a very long fin, q→M=hPkA​θb​. Past mL≈2.5 the fin delivers over 98% of that, so more length is wasted. The fin efficiency ηf​=q/(hAfin​θb​) compares the fin with an ideal one at base temperature all over; the effectiveness q/(hAθb​) compares it with no fin at all. Fins pay off when k is high, h is low and the fins are slender.

Worked exampleA CPU cooler pin

Aluminium pin, d = 3 mm, L = 30 mm, k = 200 W/(m K), fan-driven h = 40 W/(m² K), base 40 K above the air.

  1. m=hP/(kA)​=16.3299 1/m, so mL=0.4899: a short, efficient fin. The tip runs at 35.4402 K above the air.
  2. A finite-difference solve with 2001 nodes and a ghost-node tip condition matches the analytic profile to 4×10−10.
  3. Heat rate 0.42829 W, the same from the FD base gradient. Efficiency 0.9236; effectiveness 37.87, so the pin carries 38 times what its base area would without it.
  4. Longer pins: 0.85713 W at 0.1 m, 0.92334 W at 0.3 m, 0.92344 W at 1 m =hPkA​θb​, the long-fin limit.

Exercise 1A steel bolt as a fin

A 10 mm stainless-steel bolt (k = 15) sticks 50 mm out of a hot engine block, 80 K above the air, with h = 25 W/(m² K). Treat it as a long fin. Find m, mL, and the heat it carries away.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. P=π⋅0.01=0.031416 m, A=7.854×10−5 m². m=25⋅0.031416/(15⋅7.854×10−5)​=25.82 1/m.
  2. mL=1.291: not really long. tanh(1.291)=0.8594, so an adiabatic-tip estimate gives 86% of the long-fin value.
  3. Long-fin value: 25⋅0.031416⋅15⋅7.854×10−5​⋅80=2.433 W. With the adiabatic tip, about 2.433⋅0.8594=2.09 W.

Long-fin heat rate (W): h = 25, d = 10 mm, k = 15, θ_b = 80 K. 4 decimals.
Fraction of the long-fin heat rate an adiabatic-tip fin delivers at mL = 2.5 (tanh). 4 decimals.
Fins are most worthwhile when:

13.05.title: Lumped transient cooling
13.05.html:
You buy a coconut at a 30 °C roadside stall and put it in the fridge. When is it cold? If the whole coconut stayed at one uniform temperature while it cooled, the answer would be a simple exponential. Whether that is a fair assumption depends on one number, the Biot number.

The lumped model

Suppose a body of volume V, surface area A, density ρ and specific heat c is at a single temperature T(t). Its energy falls at the rate convection removes it:

ρcVdtdT​=−hA(T−T∞​)⇒Ti​−T∞​T−T∞​​=e−t/τ,τ=hAρcV​.

After one time constant τ the excess temperature is down to 36.8%, after 3τ to 5%. This is the same first-order law as an RC circuit charging.

When is it allowed?

Inside the body, heat must conduct to the surface; outside, convection carries it off. The ratio of the internal conduction resistance to the external convection resistance is the Biot number, with the characteristic length Lc​=V/A:

Bi=khLc​​.

If Bi<0.1 the inside stays within about 5% of uniform and the lumped model is accurate. A small steel part in oil passes easily. A water-filled coconut does not: water conducts poorly, so the outside cools while the centre lags.

Worked exampleCoconut and bearing ball

Assumptions. The coconut is a sphere of water, r = 6 cm (ρ = 1000, c = 4180, k = 0.6), with the shell ignored. Still fridge air at 4 °C gives h = 10 W/(m² K). It starts at 30 °C; “cold” means 8 °C.

  1. Lc​=r/3=0.02 m, so Bi=10⋅0.02/0.6=0.3333: too big for the lumped model.
  2. Lumped anyway: τ=ρcLc​/h=8360 s =2.3222 h, and the time to 8 °C is τln(26/4)=4.3467 h. An RK4 integration of the ODE lands on 8 °C to 10−9.
  3. The exact sphere solution (a 40-term series) at that moment: mean 9.4961 °C, centre 11.1005 °C. The mean actually reaches 8 °C after 5.2439 h and the centre after 5.9671 h. The lumped model is about 1.6 h optimistic about when the middle is cold.
  4. A 10 mm steel bearing ball quenched in oil (k = 45, h = 100): Bi=0.0037, τ=61.10 s, and the lumped curve stays within 8.2×10−4 of the exact mean throughout.

Exercise 1A thermocouple bead

A thermocouple bead is a 1 mm diameter sphere (ρ = 8500, c = 400, k = 20) in an air stream with h = 150 W/(m² K). Check the Biot number, find its time constant, and how long it takes to show 99% of a sudden temperature step.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Lc​=r/3=0.0005/3=1.667×10−4 m. Bi=150⋅1.667×10−4/20=0.00125: lumped is fine.
  2. τ=ρcLc​/h=8500⋅400⋅1.667×10−4/150=3.778 s.
  3. 99% means e−t/τ=0.01, so t=τln100=17.40 s.

quiz.q: Biot number of a water sphere, r = 6 cm, k = 0.6, h = 10 (L_c = r/3). 4 decimals.
Lumped time constant (s) of the thermocouple bead: ρ = 8500, c = 400, d = 1 mm, h = 150. 3 decimals.
How many time constants until 99% of a step is reached? 4 decimals.
The lumped model is reasonable when:
quiz.explain: Internal resistance must be small compared with the convective one.

quiz.q: For a body with Bi = 0.33, the lumped model predicts cooling that is:
quiz.explain: Heat has to conduct out of the middle first.

13.06.title: Distributed transient conduction
13.06.html:
When the Biot number is large, the temperature inside a body varies from place to place as it heats or cools. Think of a thick steak in a sous-vide bath: the surface reaches the bath temperature almost at once, while the middle takes most of an hour. To predict this we solve the heat equation in space and time.

The heat equation

Energy balance on a slice of a solid with no heat generation gives, in one dimension,

∂t∂T​=α∂x2∂2T​,α=ρck​.

The thermal diffusivity α sets the pace. Time enters through the Fourier number Fo=αt/L2: a body twice as thick takes four times as long.

The series solution

For a slab −L≤x≤L, initially at Ti​, with both faces suddenly held at Ts​, separation of variables gives

Ti​−Ts​T−Ts​​=n=0∑∞​(2n+1)π4(−1)n​cos(λn​x)e−λn2​αt,λn​=2L(2n+1)π​.

Higher terms decay fast, so for Fo>0.2 the first term alone is accurate. In 2D, a long square bar’s solution is the product of two slab solutions, θ(x,y,t)=θx​(x,t)θy​(y,t).

Finite differences

On a grid with spacing Δx and time step Δt, the explicit scheme updates each node from its neighbours:

Tin+1​=Tin​+r(Ti+1n​−2Tin​+Ti−1n​),r=Δx2αΔt​.

It is stable only for r≤1/2 in 1D (and r≤1/4 in 2D). Exceed that and errors grow without bound.

Worked exampleSous-vide steak

Assumptions. A 4 cm-thick steak (L=0.02 m) with water-like α=1.4×10−7 m²/s goes from 5 °C into a stirred 60 °C bath. Stirred water gives Bi > 10, so we take the faces as held at 60 °C.

  1. Bisecting on the series, the centre reaches 55 °C after 3056.4 s =50.94 min, at Fo=1.0697. The one-term series agrees to 10−5.
  2. Explicit FD with 81 nodes and r=0.4 matches the series to 5.5×10−5 in θ (centre 55.003 °C).
  3. The same grid with r=0.6 explodes to ∣θ∣≈2×1078 within 10 simulated minutes.
  4. A 4 × 4 cm square bar on a 41 × 41 grid: after 30 min its centre is at 56.032 °C against 56.019 °C from the product solution, max error 2.4×10−4.

Exercise 1A thicker cut

How long would a 6 cm-thick steak take to reach 55 °C at its centre in the same bath? Use the Fourier number, then check it with the one-term solution.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The target θ and the geometry are the same, so the same Fourier number applies: Fo=1.0697. With L=0.03 m, t=1.0697⋅0.032/1.4×10−7=6877 s =114.6 min, (3/2)2=2.25 times longer.
  2. One term: θ=(4/π)e−(π/2)2Fo=1/11 gives Fo=ln(4⋅11/π)/(π/2)2=1.0697. Same answer.

quiz.q: Fourier number αt/L² for α = 1.4e-7, t = 3600 s, L = 0.02 m. 3 decimals.
Largest stable time step (s) for explicit 1D FD with Δx = 0.5 mm and α = 1.4e-7. 4 decimals.
One-term slab solution, centre θ at Fo = 0.5. 5 decimals.
Doubling the thickness of a slab makes the time to reach the same centre temperature:
quiz.explain: Fo = αt/L² must stay the same.

quiz.q: For a long square bar, the 2D transient solution equals:

13.07.title: Convection and the boundary layer
13.07.html:
Blow on hot soup and it cools faster. The moving air sweeps away the warm layer next to the surface and brings cooler air closer. Convection is conduction into a fluid that is moving, and the key to it is the thin thermal boundary layer where the temperature changes from the wall value to the free-stream value.

Newton’s law of cooling and the Nusselt number

Engineers lump all the fluid mechanics into one coefficient h:

q′′=h(Tw​−T∞​).

h is not a property of the fluid; it depends on speed, geometry and position. Right at the wall the fluid is still, so heat crosses by conduction, q′′=−k∂T/∂y∣w​. Comparing the two gives the dimensionless Nusselt number, the wall temperature gradient relative to a plain conduction gradient over length L:

Nu=khL​.

Three numbers control it: the Reynolds number Re=UL/ν, the Prandtl number Pr=ν/α (momentum diffusion against heat diffusion: 0.7 for air, about 4 to 7 for water), and the geometry.

Laminar flow over a flat plate

The Blasius velocity profile from 12.11 carries heat. With η=yU/(νx)​ and θ=(T−Tw​)/(T∞​−Tw​), the energy equation becomes the Pohlhausen equation,

θ′′+21​Prfθ′=0,θ(0)=0, θ(∞)=1.

Its solution gives the local and average Nusselt numbers for laminar flow (Re<5×105):

Nux​=0.332Rex1/2​Pr1/3,NuL​=0.664ReL1/2​Pr1/3.

The local h falls as x−1/2 because the boundary layer thickens, and the average over the plate is twice the trailing-edge value. Beyond transition the turbulent layer mixes harder: Nux​=0.0296Rex0.8​Pr1/3.

Worked exampleDeriving 0.332 and cooling a solar panel

  1. RK4 shooting on the Blasius equation gives f′′(0)=0.332057.
  2. Integrating the Pohlhausen equation on that profile gives Nux​/Rex1/2​=0.29268 at Pr = 0.7, 0.33206 at Pr = 1, 0.57669 at Pr = 5 and 0.72814 at Pr = 10. The fit 0.332Pr1/3 gives 0.29478, 0.33200, 0.56771 and 0.71527: within 2%. At Pr = 1, θ=f′ exactly (the Reynolds analogy).
  3. A 0.5 m solar panel in a 3 m/s breeze of 30 °C air (ν=1.608×10−5, k=0.02588, Pr = 0.7282): ReL​=93284, laminar. Nu=182.454, hˉ=9.4438 W/(m² K), and at 25 K above the air the top surface sheds 118.048 W per metre of width. Averaging the local h numerically gives 9.4375, and the trailing-edge local value is 4.7219, half the average.

Exercise 1A laptop lid

A laptop lid 0.3 m deep sits in a 2 m/s air stream at 30 °C, 15 K warmer than the air. Find ReL​, the average h, and the heat lost from 0.3 × 0.2 m of one side.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ReL​=2⋅0.3/1.608×10−5=37313, laminar.
  2. Nu=0.664⋅373131/2⋅0.72821/3=115.39, so hˉ=115.39⋅0.02588/0.3=9.955 W/(m² K).
  3. Q=9.955⋅0.06⋅15=8.96 W.

13.08.title: Forced convection in pipes
13.08.html:
Coolant in an engine, water in a solar collector, refrigerant in an air conditioner: most heat exchange happens inside tubes. For these flows we rarely solve the equations. We use correlations, curve fits to experiments. Each one comes with a validity range, and using it outside that range is one of the most common mistakes in thermal design.

Laminar flow: exact limits

Below Re=UD/ν≈2300 the flow is laminar. Far enough downstream, the shape of the temperature profile stops changing (thermally fully developed), and the Nusselt number Nu=hD/k becomes a constant:

Nu=3.66  (constant wall temperature),Nu=1148​=4.36  (constant heat flux).

Both follow from the energy equation with the parabolic velocity profile u=2U(1−r2/rw2​). The 3.66 is an eigenvalue: Nu=λ2/2, where λ makes ϕ′′+ϕ′/r+λ2(1−r2)ϕ=0 vanish at the wall.

Turbulent flow: correlations

Dittus-Boelter, simple and widely quoted:

Nu=0.023Re0.8Prn,n=0.4 heating, 0.3 cooling

valid for Re>104, 0.6<Pr<160, L/D>10, and modest temperature differences.

Gnielinski, more accurate (about 10%) and valid down into the transition range:

Nu=1+12.7f/8​(Pr2/3−1)(f/8)(Re−1000)Pr​,f=(0.790lnRe−1.64)−2

for 3000<Re<5×106 and 0.5<Pr<2000. Between 2300 and 3000, no correlation is trustworthy.

Worked exampleLaminar limits and a coolant loop

  1. Shooting on the eigenvalue problem gives Nu=3.6568; integrating the constant-flux temperature profile numerically gives 4.3636 =48/11.
  2. Water at 40 °C (ν=0.658×10−6, k=0.631, Pr = 4.32) in a 10 mm tube at 1 m/s, being heated: Re=15198, inside both ranges. Dittus-Boelter gives Nu = 91.48 (h=5773 W/(m² K)); Gnielinski 95.98 (h=6056). They agree within 5%.
  3. At Re = 4000, Dittus-Boelter (outside its range) gives 31.45 against Gnielinski’s 26.74: 18% too high.

Exercise 1Air in a duct

Air at 40 °C (ν=1.70×10−5, k=0.0271, Pr = 0.71) flows at 5 m/s through a 50 mm duct and is heated. Find Re and h from Dittus-Boelter. Is it in range?

Show step-by-step solution

  2. Nu=0.023⋅147060.8⋅0.710.4=43.27.

13.09.title: Natural convection
13.09.html:
A radiator heats a room with no fan. Air next to the hot panel warms, becomes less dense, and rises; cool air slides in below to replace it. This is natural (or free) convection: the flow is driven by buoyancy, so the fluid speed is not something you set, it is an outcome of the temperature difference.

Grashof and Rayleigh

The buoyancy force per unit volume is about ρgβΔT, where β is the thermal expansion coefficient (β=1/T for an ideal gas, with T in kelvin). Comparing buoyancy with viscous forces gives the Grashof number; multiplying by Pr gives the Rayleigh number, which plays the role Re plays in forced convection:

Gr=ν2gβΔTL3​,Ra=GrPr=ναgβΔTL3​.

For a vertical plate, L is the height. The boundary layer stays laminar up to about Ra≈109 and becomes turbulent above.

The vertical plate

For laminar flow, the boundary-layer equations have a similarity solution (Ostrach, 1953). With η=(y/x)(Grx​/4)1/4:

F′′′+3FF′′−2F′2+θ=0,θ′′+3PrFθ′=0,

and the wall gradient θ′(0) gives NuL​=34​(GrL​/4)1/4(−θ′(0)), which scales as Ra1/4. In practice, use the Churchill-Chu correlation, valid for all Ra:

NuL​={0.825+[1+(0.492/Pr)9/16]8/270.387Ra1/6​}2,

with a slightly more accurate laminar version for Ra<109: NuL​=0.68+0.670Ra1/4/[1+(0.492/Pr)9/16]4/9. The simple fits 0.59Ra1/4 (laminar) and 0.10Ra1/3 (turbulent) are good for estimates. Natural-convection coefficients in air are small, typically 2 to 10 W/(m² K).

Worked exampleOstrach’s numbers, a radiator and a sunny wall

  1. Newton shooting on the two unknown wall values gives, at Pr = 0.72, F′′(0)=0.6760 and −θ′(0)=0.5046, matching Ostrach’s table. At Pr = 0.71: 0.6775 and 0.5021.
  2. That gives NuL​=0.5157Ra1/4; the Churchill-Chu laminar coefficient is 0.5142, within 0.3%.
  3. A 0.6 m radiator panel at 60 °C in a 20 °C room, air at the 40 °C film temperature (ν=1.70×10−5, k=0.0271, Pr = 0.71, β=1/313.15): Ra=6.6495×108, laminar. Nu = 83.259, h=3.7605 W/(m² K), and each face convects 90.25 W per metre of width (the rest of its output is radiation).
  4. A 3 m wall in the sun, 25 K above the air: Ra=5.1949×1010, turbulent. Churchill-Chu gives Nu = 426.09 and h=3.8490; the simple 0.10Ra1/3 gives 373.13.

Exercise 1A hot oven door

An oven door 0.5 m tall is at 50 °C in a 20 °C kitchen. With air at the 35 °C film (ν=1.65×10−5, α=2.34×10−5, k=0.0268, Pr = 0.71, β=1/308.15), find Ra, then h from the simple laminar fit 0.59Ra1/4.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Ra=9.81⋅(1/308.15)⋅30⋅0.53/(1.65×10−5⋅2.34×10−5)=3.0920×108, laminar.
  2. Nu=0.59⋅(3.0920×108)1/4=78.24.
  3. h=78.24⋅0.0268/0.5=4.19 W/(m² K).

13.10.title: Radiation
13.10.html:
Stand in the sun and you feel the warmth even on a cool day. No air carries that heat: it arrives as electromagnetic radiation, the only mode of heat transfer that works through a vacuum. Every surface above absolute zero emits radiation, and the amount rises steeply with temperature.

Emission

A perfect emitter, a black body, radiates Eb​=σT4 with σ=5.670×10−8 W/(m² K⁴) and T in kelvin. Real surfaces emit a fraction ε, the emissivity:

E=εσT4.

Absorptivity α is the fraction of incoming radiation absorbed. For the same wavelengths, α=ε (Kirchhoff’s law). But sunlight is short-wave (peaking near 0.5 µm) while a roof emits long-wave infrared (near 10 µm), so a surface can have very different solar absorptivity and thermal emissivity. White paint absorbs little sun but emits strongly; bare galvanised steel absorbs a lot of sun and emits poorly, so it gets very hot.

View factors

How much radiation leaving surface 1 reaches surface 2 depends on geometry, captured by the view factor F12​, the fraction of diffusely emitted energy that lands on 2:

F12​=A1​1​∫A1​​∫A2​​πs2cosθ1​cosθ2​​dA2​dA1​.

It obeys reciprocity, A1​F12​=A2​F21​, and the summation rule ∑j​F1j​=1. For two large parallel plates close together, F12​→1. A Monte Carlo estimate is direct: fire random rays from surface 1, with a cosine-weighted direction, and count the fraction that hit surface 2.

Exchange between grey surfaces

For two large parallel grey plates, net exchange per unit area is

q′′=1/ε1​+1/ε2​−1σ(T14​−T24​)​.

A single low-emissivity surface, such as foil under a roof, cuts the exchange dramatically.

Worked exampleView factors and a tropical roof

  1. Unit squares 1 m apart: one million Monte Carlo rays give F=0.2002 against the exact 0.1998 (standard error 4×10−4). At 0.1 m: 0.8272 against 0.8270. At 0.01 m: 0.9802 against 0.9804, heading to 1.
  2. A steel roof at 70 °C over a ceiling at 35 °C: with both surfaces painted (ε=0.9), 224.95 W/m² radiates down. Foil under the roof (ε=0.05) cuts it to 13.67 W/m².
  3. Assumptions. A roof in Bali at noon: 1000 W/m² of sun, air 31 °C, effective sky 21 °C, h=10 W/(m² K), underside insulated. Galvanised steel (absorptivity 0.65, emissivity 0.25) reaches 83.64 °C; dark paint (0.90, 0.90) 79.91 °C; white cool-roof paint (0.20, 0.90) only 40.08 °C.

Exercise 1Two plates

Two large parallel plates are at 400 K (ε=0.8) and 300 K (ε=0.6). Find the net radiative flux. What does it become if both were black?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. σ(T14​−T24​)=5.670×10−8(4004−3004)=992.3 W/m².
  2. Denominator 1/0.8+1/0.6−1=1.9167, so q′′=992.3/1.9167=517.7 W/m².
  3. Black plates: 992.3 W/m².

13.11.title: Solar energy
13.11.html:
A solar panel on a Bali rooftop and one in Zürich see the same Sun but harvest very different amounts of energy. How much a surface collects depends on where the Sun is in the sky, which depends on latitude, the day of the year and the time of day. This geometry is the first step in sizing any solar collector or panel.

Where is the Sun?

The Earth’s axis is tilted 23.45°, so the latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon, the declination δ, swings through the year. A good approximation (Cooper) for day number n:

δ=23.45∘sin(360∘365284+n​).

The hour angle ω=15∘ per hour from solar noon. The Sun’s elevation above the horizon αs​ at latitude φ is

sinαs​=sinφsinδ+cosφcosδcosω.

At noon (ω=0) this collapses to αnoon​=90∘−∣φ−δ∣. In the northern hemisphere with the Sun to the south, that is 90∘−φ+δ.

How much energy arrives?

Outside the atmosphere the beam carries the solar constant, about 1361 W/m². A horizontal surface intercepts Gsinαs​. Integrating over the day from sunrise to sunset (cosωs​=−tanφtanδ) gives the daily extraterrestrial total:

H0​=π24​Gsc​(cosφcosδsinωs​+ωs​sinφsinδ).

The atmosphere absorbs and scatters more when the Sun is low, because the light crosses more air (the air mass is about 1/sinαs​). A simple clear-sky model (Meinel) for the direct beam is 1353⋅0.7AM0.678 W/m², to which we add about 10% for diffuse sky light. Clouds then cut the real total well below the clear-sky figure.

Worked exampleBali against Zürich

Latitudes: Denpasar 8.65° S (φ=−8.65∘), Zürich 47.37° N.

  1. On 21 June (δ=+23.450∘), the noon Sun stands at 57.900° in Bali (in the northern sky) and 66.080° in Zürich. On 21 December (δ=−23.450∘): 75.200° in Bali, only 19.180° in Zürich. A minute-by-minute search of the day confirms each noon value matches 90∘−∣φ−δ∣ to 10−6 degrees.
  2. Numerically integrating Gsc​sinαs​ over each day matches the analytic H0​ to within 1 Wh/m².
  3. Clear-sky days: Zürich gets 8.090 kWh/m² on a horizontal panel in June but 1.051 in December, a ratio of 7.70. Bali gets 5.633 in June and 7.216 in December.
  4. Over a clear-sky year: 2480 kWh/m² in Bali, 1621 in Zürich. A 20% efficient panel makes 496 and 324 kWh/m². Real totals are lower (clouds), but the ratio holds roughly.

Exercise 1Noon in Bali and Zürich at the equinox

On the March equinox (δ=0), find the noon elevation and the clear-sky direct beam at noon (Meinel, air mass 1/sinαs​) in Bali and in Zürich.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Bali: 90−8.65=81.35∘. AM =1/sin81.35∘=1.0115, beam =1353⋅0.71.01150.678=944.5 W/m².
  2. Zürich: 90−47.37=42.63∘. AM =1.4765, beam =1353⋅0.71.47670.678=850.3 W/m².
  3. On a horizontal surface, multiply by sinαs​: 933.7 and 575.8 W/m².

13.12.title: Heat exchangers and the LMTD
13.12.html:
A car radiator, an oil cooler, the condenser on an air conditioner: a heat exchanger moves heat from one flowing fluid to another through a wall. The design question is usually “how much area do I need?”, and the answer depends heavily on which way the two fluids flow.

The basic balance

With the hot stream’s capacity rate Ch​=m˙h​ch​ (W/K) and the cold stream’s Cc​, energy conservation gives

Q=Ch​(Th,in​−Th,out​)=Cc​(Tc,out​−Tc,in​).

Through the wall, heat flows at UdA(Th​−Tc​) locally, where U is the overall heat transfer coefficient (a resistance network, as in 13.02). The temperature difference changes along the exchanger, so we need the right average.

Log mean temperature difference

Integrating the two stream equations along the exchanger gives exactly

Q=UAΔTlm​,ΔTlm​=ln(ΔT1​/ΔT2​)ΔT1​−ΔT2​​,

where ΔT1​ and ΔT2​ are the hot-minus-cold differences at the two ends. In parallel flow both fluids enter at the same end: ΔT1​=Th,in​−Tc,in​, ΔT2​=Th,out​−Tc,out​. In counterflow they enter at opposite ends: ΔT1​=Th,in​−Tc,out​, ΔT2​=Th,out​−Tc,in​.

For the same inlet and outlet temperatures, the counterflow LMTD is always larger, so it needs less area. Counterflow can even heat the cold stream above the hot stream’s outlet temperature, which parallel flow never can.

Worked exampleAn oil cooler

Engine oil enters at 110 °C with Ch​=0.2⋅2100=420 W/K; cooling water enters at 25 °C with Cc​=0.1⋅4180=418 W/K. UA=300 W/K.

  1. Marching both streams along the area with RK4 (parallel), and shooting on the water outlet (counterflow):
    • Parallel: oil out 77.7276 °C, water out 57.4268 °C, Q=13554.397 W. UAΔTlm​ with ΔTlm​=45.1813 K gives the same 13554.397 W.
    • Counter: oil out 74.6186 °C, water out 60.5507 °C, Q=14860.179 W, ΔTlm​=49.5339 K, again matching.
  2. Fixed duty: cool the oil to 80 °C (Q=12600 W), so the water leaves at 55.1435 °C. Parallel needs UA=257.59 W/K; counterflow 229.39 W/K, 10.9% less area. Marching the counterflow exchanger with that UA brings the oil to 80 °C to 10−4 K.

Exercise 1Sizing a water heater

A counterflow exchanger heats 0.05 kg/s of water (c = 4180) from 15 °C to 55 °C using hot water entering at 85 °C and leaving at 50 °C. U = 800 W/(m² K). Find Q, the LMTD and the area. What area would parallel flow need?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Q=0.05⋅4180⋅40=8360 W.
  2. Counter: ΔT1​=85−55=30, ΔT2​=50−15=35. ΔTlm​=5/ln(35/30)=32.44 K. A=8360/(800⋅32.44)=0.3222 m².
  3. Parallel: ΔT1​=85−15=70, ΔT2​=50−55=−5. The cold outlet would have to exceed the hot outlet: impossible in parallel flow.

13.13.title: The effectiveness-NTU method
13.13.html:
The LMTD method is ideal when you know all four temperatures and want the area. Often it is the other way round: you have an exchanger (you know UA) and want to know what it will do with given inlet temperatures. With LMTD that means guessing an outlet temperature and iterating. The effectiveness-NTU method answers directly.

Effectiveness

The most heat any exchanger could transfer is limited by the stream with the smaller capacity rate Cmin​, which could at best change temperature by the full inlet difference:

Qmax​=Cmin​(Th,in​−Tc,in​),ε=Qmax​Q​.

NTU and capacity ratio

Two dimensionless groups determine ε for a given flow arrangement: the number of transfer units and the capacity ratio,

NTU=Cmin​UA​,Cr​=Cmax​Cmin​​.

Solving the same stream equations as for LMTD gives closed forms:

εparallel​=1+Cr​1−e−NTU(1+Cr​)​,εcounter​=1−Cr​e−NTU(1−Cr​)1−e−NTU(1−Cr​)​,

with εcounter​=NTU/(1+NTU) when Cr​=1. When one stream condenses or boils, its temperature stays constant (Cr​=0) and every arrangement gives ε=1−e−NTU.

Two lessons hide in these formulas. Parallel flow can never beat 1/(1+Cr​), only 50% for balanced streams. And past NTU of about 3, extra area buys very little.

Worked exampleThe oil cooler again

  1. For four exchangers with different Ch​, Cc​ and UA, marching the streams with RK4 reproduces both closed-form effectivenesses to a worst relative error of 4.4×10−14.
  2. The 13.12 oil cooler: Cmin​=418 W/K (water), so NTU=300/418=0.7177 and Cr​=418/420=0.9952. Parallel: ε=0.38149, Q=13554.397 W. Counter: ε=0.41824, Q=14860.179 W. Both match UAΔTlm​ exactly, with no iteration.
  3. Balanced counterflow: ε=0.3333, 0.5000, 0.6667, 0.8000, 0.8889 at NTU 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8. Parallel flow: 0.3161, 0.4323, 0.4908, 0.4998, 0.5000, stuck at one half.

Exercise 1A shower heat recovery pipe

Waste shower water at 38 °C runs down a counterflow drain heat exchanger, warming incoming mains water at 15 °C. Both flows are 0.12 kg/s (c = 4180) and UA=600 W/K. Find NTU, the effectiveness, the heat recovered and the preheated water temperature.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. C=0.12⋅4180=501.6 W/K for both streams, so Cr​=1 and NTU=600/501.6=1.1962.
  2. ε=1.1962/2.1962=0.5447.
  3. Q=0.5447⋅501.6⋅23=6284 W.
  4. The mains water leaves at 15+0.5447⋅23=27.53 °C.

13.14.title: E-bike battery thermal model
13.14.html:
Lithium-ion cells age quickly when hot and must not be discharged above about 60 °C. On a Bali afternoon the air is already at 32 °C, and a long climb pulls high current. Will the pack overheat? In this project we build a thermal model of an e-bike battery from the pieces of this phase: heat generation, a resistance network, thermal mass and convection.

The model

Heat generation. The pack’s internal resistance turns electrical power into heat: Q˙​=I2Rpack​. A 36 V pack of 10 cells in series and 5 in parallel (10s5p), with 45 mΩ cells, has Rpack​=10⋅0.045/5=0.09 Ω.

Two nodes. The cells (with holders, Ccells​=2.3⋅900=2070 J/K) sit inside an aluminium case (Ccase​=0.6⋅900=540 J/K). Heat crosses foam and air gaps to the case through Rint​=0.25 K/W, then convects from the case’s 0.12 m² into the air with h=15 W/(m² K) while riding and 5 when parked:

Ccells​dtdTcells​​=I2Rpack​−Rint​Tcells​−Tcase​​,Ccase​dtdTcase​​=Rint​Tcells​−Tcase​​−hA(Tcase​−T∞​).

This is an RC circuit with two capacitors. In steady state the capacitors stop mattering and the temperature rise is simply heat times the series resistance:

Tcells​−T∞​=I2Rpack​(Rint​+hA1​).

The two time constants come from the eigenvalues of the 2 × 2 system: a fast one for the light case and a slow one for the whole pack.

Worked exampleA climb on a hot afternoon

Assumptions. The pack values above, air at 32 °C, cells starting at air temperature, and heat generation from internal resistance only (no entropic heat, constant resistance).

  1. Constant 15 A: Q˙​=20.250 W and Rtotal​=0.25+1/(15⋅0.12)=0.8056 K/W, so the network predicts cells at 48.312 °C and the case at 43.250 °C. A 10-hour RK4 simulation settles at 48.3125 and 43.2500 °C.
  2. Time constants: 31.42 min for the pack and 1.37 min for the case.
  3. A ride: 20 min flat at 10 A, a 15 min climb at 25 A, 25 min rolling at 8 A, then 30 min parked. The cells peak at 51.474 °C at the top of the climb, 35.00 min in, and cool to 39.428 °C by 90 min. Holding 25 A indefinitely would settle at 32+625⋅0.09⋅0.8056=77.3 °C: only the thermal mass keeps this climb safe.
  4. Energy check: the 70065.0 J generated equals 18952.7 J stored plus 51112.3 J convected.

Exercise 1How long a climb is safe?

With the same pack starting at 32 °C, approximate the pack as a single lump (C=2610 J/K, R=0.8056 K/W). How long can it sustain 30 A before the cells reach 60 °C?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Steady rise at 30 A: Q˙​=900⋅0.09=81 W, so ΔT∞​=81⋅0.8056=65.25 K.
  2. Time constant τ=RC=0.8056⋅2610=2102.6 s =35.04 min.
  3. 28=65.25(1−e−t/τ) gives t=−τln(1−28/65.25)=0.5605τ=1179 s, about 19.6 min. The two-node model says slightly less, because the cells heat before the case does.
